title: X Feed Digest
summary: The clearest AI theme was the shift from chat to delegated work: Grok Build, Gemini Spark, and vertical voice interfaces all pushed toward background agents rather than one-shot assistants.

The workflow conversation got more disciplined: cross-model review patterns, Codex-vs-Claude efficiency chatter, and vibe-coding warnings all pointed to reliability and cost control mattering more than novelty.
The most actionable data launch in the batch was Dune's unified Kalshi + Polymarket dataset, which makes prediction markets easier to study as real research inputs instead of isolated apps.
Market commentary was thinner than AI, but one durable macro thread stood out: AI beneficiaries may include power-, mineral-, and land-rich geographies like Brazil, not just model vendors.
A more sobering undercurrent kept surfacing too: stronger AI tooling can reduce headcount just as easily as it boosts output, and blindly trusting a single model can go sideways fast.

items.title: @xai: Grok Build Beta Widens
items.body: xAI opened Grok Build beta to SuperGrok and X Premium+ users with planning mode, image/video generation, CLI automations, and orchestration hooks. The bigger signal is X moving from chatbot access toward a full agent-builder surface inside its consumer subscription stack.

items.title: @GeminiApp: Spark as a Background Agent
items.body: Google framed Gemini Spark as a 24/7 agent that keeps working even when your devices are off and checks back before major actions. That's a meaningful product shift: the frontier is moving from answer quality toward trustworthy delegated execution.

items.title: @EvidenceOpen: Voice Mode for Doctors
items.body: OpenEvidence launched a multimodal voice interface for clinicians that keeps peer-reviewed citations while making responses short enough for rounds and hallway use. It's a good example of vertical AI winning by fitting a real workflow instead of just adding generic chat.

items.title: @getsome_air: Cross-Model Code Review Pattern
items.body: One practical workflow tip stood out: let one model implement code and a different model review it, leave comments, and hand fixes back. It's a clean way to get some multi-agent upside without letting multiple writers stomp on the same codebase.

items.title: @heykeithbrown: Codex Usage Growth Speeds Up
items.body: A usage tracker covering 100-plus AI-native developers said Codex usage is growing faster than Claude Code even though Claude still leads overall share. Small sample caveat aside, it matches the broader feed mood: teams are optimizing harder for speed, reliability, and token efficiency.

items.title: @Dune: Unified Kalshi + Polymarket Data
items.body: Dune launched a combined Kalshi and Polymarket dataset with hourly candles, per-fill trades, and warehouse export paths into Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks. For macro or event-driven researchers, this meaningfully lowers the friction to compare pricing and liquidity across the two main prediction-market venues.

items.title: @drewcrawford_: Brazil as an AI-Adjacent Asset Bet
items.body: A detailed Brazil thread argued that U.S. allocators still under-own a country with farmland, freshwater, clean power, niobium, and offshore oil in one package. Whether or not you buy the full bull case, it was a sharp reminder that AI beneficiaries may include resource-heavy geographies, not just software names.

items.title: @LabSpeculation: Cross-Check Strange LLM Output
items.body: A widely shared cautionary post argued that a flattering assistant can reinforce bad beliefs instead of challenging them, and that switching models can break the spell. The practical takeaway is solid: for anything high-stakes or weird, force a second-model or human sanity check.

items.title: @Matt_Graham_: Vibe Coding Debt Still Counts
items.body: A builder-services thread made the case that AI can get you to a working demo faster than it gets you to a maintainable product. The useful point wasn't anti-AI; it was that structure, review, and refactoring still have to happen somewhere.

items.title: @shao__meng: AI Efficiency Can Become Layoff Math
items.body: One blunt anecdote described a team proving strong productivity gains with large Cursor budgets and then getting cut because management concluded fewer developers were needed. Crude as it is, it captures a real near-term risk: tooling wins do not automatically accrue to the people using the tools.
